cve_summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in the safe_fprintf function in tar/util.c in libarchive 3.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted non-printable multibyte character in a filename.
commit_message:
Issue #767:  Buffer overflow printing a filename

The safe_fprintf function attempts to ensure clean output for an
arbitrary sequence of bytes by doing a trial conversion of the
multibyte characters to wide characters -- if the resulting wide
character is printable then we pass through the corresponding bytes
unaltered, otherwise, we convert them to C-style ASCII escapes.

The stack trace in Issue #767 suggest that the 20-byte buffer
was getting overflowed trying to format a non-printable multibyte
character.  This should only happen if there is a valid multibyte
character of more than 5 bytes that was unprintable.  (Each byte
would get expanded to a four-charcter octal-style escape of the form
"\123" resulting in >20 characters for the >5 byte multibyte character.)

I've not been able to reproduce this, but have expanded the conversion
buffer to 128 bytes on the belief that no multibyte character set
has a single character of more than 32 bytes.
docstring:
"""
Summary: 
Prints a formatted string to a specified file, handling non-printable characters safely.

Parameters: 
f (FILE *): The file stream to which the formatted string will be printed.
fmt (const char *): The format string used for printing, followed by variable arguments.

Returns: 
None: This function does not return a value.

Logic: 
The function uses a stack-allocated buffer for formatting the string to optimize performance and safety. It attempts to format the string using `vsnprintf`, and if the buffer is too small, it allocates a larger heap buffer. It checks for printable wide characters using `mbtowc` and expands unprintable characters accordingly. The output is printed in chunks to avoid buffer overflow. Finally, any allocated heap memory is freed before the function exits.
"""
